title: The Quickest Way to Expand School Choice Is to Fill Empty Private School Seats rivate-school-seats
author: Kathleen Porter-Magee
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Flypaper (fordhaminstitute.org), September 17, 2026
summary: Kathleen Porter-Magee argues that the rapid spread of private school choice, with 18 states now offering universal or near-universal programs and 27 opting into the federal scholarship tax credit starting in 2027, has created a supply problem that new-school start-ups alone cannot solve quickly. She proposes a three-tiered supply strategy: filling excess capacity in existing schools, scaling thriving schools and networks, and seeding new schools where supply is genuinely scarce, and insists the first tier is the fastest and most cost-effective. Much of that spare capacity sits in Catholic schools, whose enrollment declined for decades because of tuition-free charter competition, the shift from religious to salaried lay staff, and philanthropy that bypassed parochial schools. Florida serves as the proof case: private schools operating at 79 percent capacity in 2022 added more than 80,000 students by 2024, and Catholic enrollment rose 19 percent through diocesan marketing, new program offerings, and reopened schools, with early signs of similar gains in Texas. Her closing move is to frame existing-school growth as a modest, time-limited investment without land, leases, or new construction, making the first question in every state where good schools with room to grow are located.
points: Porter-Magee's three-tier supply model (fill existing seats, scale strong schools, seed new ones) treats venture-backed start-ups as important but too slow for today's surge in demand.

Catholic school enrollment shrank for two decades due to charter competition, the move from religious to paid lay staff, and philanthropic investment that flowed to district and charter sectors instead.

Florida private schools went from 79 percent capacity with room for 84,442 more students in 2022 to private enrollment growth of nearly 20 percent between 2021 and 2024, far outpacing a 4 percent rise in school-age population.
Dioceses drove the gains with aggressive family outreach, such as the Diocese of Venice's million-plus texts and emails, plus new dual-language, classical, and special-needs programs.
Growing existing schools avoids land acquisition, lease negotiation, and new construction, requiring only retrofitting, systems support, and targeted outreach.
quotes: Taken together, these policy developments have created an unprecedented opportunity to tap into the demand for and increase access to a private school education, particularly among families who previously were unable to afford one.
For those looking to ramp up quickly, we must acknowledge that the first tier provides the best and most cost-effective way to grow private schools quickly.

A number of internal and external factors have contributed to the decline, including a dramatic increase in tuition-free competition from the charter school sector; an internal shift in staffing structure from one that relied heavily on religious men and women to one that required a far greater number of lay (and salaried) faculty, staff, and leadership; and a policy and philanthropic environment that has, for decades, funneled billions to seed growth and operations in the district and charter sectors, while the private and parochial school sectors were largely left out.

Specifically, while the overall population of school-aged children (ages 5–17) increased by 4 percent between 2021 and 2024, private school enrollment increased by nearly 20 percent (more than 80,000 students). And these gains were driven largely by intentional efforts to fill vacant Catholic school seats.
These early examples suggest how existing schools, supported by organized outreach and practical assistance, can respond quickly when new public funding makes tuition affordable.

There’s no land acquisition. There are no complex leases to negotiate. There’s little or no new bricks-and-mortar required, just some retrofitting and modernizing work that can be done relatively quickly.
